issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave, can review the Election Tribunal's finding on the commencement of a candidate's candidature.

law.law_text: The commencement of a candidate's candidature is a question of fact.
The determination of a question of fact is the responsibility of the Election Tribunal.

application.law_text: The commencement of a candidate's candidature is a question of fact.
application.applied_to: The issue of when the appellant's candidature began was a factual determination.

application.law_text: The determination of a question of fact is the responsibility of the Election Tribunal.
application.applied_to: The Supreme Court stated that the Tribunal's decision on this question of fact is not liable to be reviewed by the Supreme Court in an appeal by special leave.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the commencement of a candidate's candidature is a question of fact to be determined by the Election Tribunal. Therefore, the Tribunal's decision on this matter is not subject to review by the Supreme Court in an appeal by special leave.

issue.issue_text: Whether a party to an election petition is entitled to a further notice under the proviso to section 99(1)(a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, before a finding of a corrupt practice is recorded, when the charge was already the subject-matter of the enquiry in the petition itself.

facts: The appellant was a party to an election petition where specific charges of corrupt practice were the subject of the enquiry.
The Election Tribunal recorded a finding against the appellant under section 99(1)(a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, for committing a corrupt practice.
The appellant argued that this finding was invalid because he was not given a separate notice as required by the proviso to section 99 before the finding was recorded.
law: The Supreme Court referred to its own precedent in a previous case (Civil Appeal No. 21 of 1955).

This precedent established that a party is not entitled to a further notice under the proviso to section 99(1)(a) if they have already had an opportunity during the hearing of the election petition to defend against the very charge on which the finding is based.
application: The Court observed that in the present case, the finding of corrupt practice under section 99(1)(a) was related to the very same payments that were the subject-matter of the enquiry in the election petition.
Since the charge was already central to the petition, the appellant had been given a full opportunity to meet and defend against it during the hearing.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that no further notice was required. Because the appellant had already had the opportunity to address the specific charge of corrupt practice during the main enquiry of the election petition, he was not entitled to a second notice on the same matter under the proviso to section 99(1)(a).

issue.issue_text: Whether the determination of a payment as a donation, an act of charity, or an election expense is a question of fact to be decided by the Tribunal.

facts: An appellant made a payment of Rs. 500 to the North Arcot District Congress Committee on September 23, 1951, shortly before an election.
The appellant contended that this payment was a donation made out of philanthropic motives.
The opposing party argued it was an election expense intended to influence the election.

The Tribunal examined the facts, including the timing of the payment, the appellant's known application for party nomination, and how the committee used the funds, and concluded the payment was for election purposes.
law: A payment made at or on the eve of an election, even if labeled a donation or an act of charity, is open to the charge that its real purpose was to induce voters to vote for the donor.
The key factor in determining the nature of the payment is the motive behind it.
application: The Supreme Court stated that whether a specific payment is a donation, an act of charity, or an election expense depends on whether it was made to induce voters to vote for the donor.
The Court held that this determination is a "question of fact to be decided by the Tribunal."

Applying this principle to the case, the Court affirmed that it was a question of fact for the Tribunal to decide if the appellant's Rs. 500 payment was a "pure act of charity or was expense incurred for election purposes."
The Court deferred to the Tribunal's factual conclusion, stating that no grounds had been shown to differ from its finding that the payment was not innocent and was motivated by the election.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that determining whether a payment is a donation, an act of charity, or an election expense is a question of fact. This determination is based on the motive behind the payment, which is a matter for the Tribunal, as the fact-finding body, to decide based on the specific circumstances of the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Tribunal erred in recording a finding of disqualification under section 140 without giving a separate notice as required by the proviso to section 99.

facts: The appellant was a party to the election petition.
The Tribunal recorded a finding that the appellant was subject to disqualification under section 140 due to a corrupt practice.
The appellant argued that this finding was invalid because the Tribunal did not give him a separate notice as required by the proviso to section 99.
law: The Court cited a previous decision (Civil Appeal No. 21 of 1955) which established a key principle.

The principle is that if a party to an election petition has already been given an opportunity during the hearing of the petition to defend against the very charge that leads to a disqualification finding, then that party is not entitled to a further, separate notice under the proviso to section 99 regarding the same matter.
application: The Court noted that the finding of disqualification under section 99(1)(a) was based on the very same payments and corrupt practices that were the central subject-matter of the election petition.
The appellant had a full opportunity to address and defend against these charges during the main hearing of the petition.
reasoning.conclusion: Because the appellant had already had the opportunity to meet the charges that formed the basis for his disqualification, the Court held that a separate notice under the proviso to section 99 was not required. Therefore, the Tribunal did not err, and the appellant's objection was rejected.

cases.principle: The determining factor for when a person's candidature commences is the decision of the candidate himself to hold himself out as a prospective candidate, not the act of other persons or bodies adopting him as their candidate.

If a party had an opportunity during the hearing of an election petition to meet the very charge for which a finding is to be recorded under section 99(1)(a), then that party is not entitled to a further notice under the proviso to that section regarding the same matter.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: There is no presumption in Hindu Law that a business standing in the name of a member of the Hindu joint family is a joint family business. While debts contracted by the father in such a business are binding on the sons on the theory of a son's pious obligation to pay his father's debt, those contracted by a manager are not binding on the other members. Furthermore, the commencement of candidature is a question of fact to be determined by the Tribunal, and its decision is not liable to be reviewed by the Supreme Court in an appeal by special leave.
obiter: But this decision could not be safely followed except where the facts are precisely similar.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court held that it will not review an Election Tribunal's findings of fact, such as the commencement of candidature or the characterization of a payment as an election expense, in an appeal by special leave. Furthermore, a party to an election petition who has already had a full opportunity to defend against a charge of corrupt practice during the main inquiry is not entitled to a separate, additional notice under the proviso to section 99(1)(a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, before the Tribunal records a finding on that same charge.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a particular sum paid at the time or on the eve of the election was a donation, an act of charity or an election expense must depend on whether or not such payment was open to the charge of having been made in order to induce the voters to vote in favour of the donor. This is a question of fact to be decided by the Tribunal.

If a party had an opportunity given to him in the hearing of the petition to meet the very charge in respect of which a finding is to be recorded under section 99(1)(a), then he is not entitled to a further notice in respect of the same matter, under the proviso.
why_appellant_lost: The Supreme Court refused to review the Tribunal's finding on the commencement of the appellant's candidature, stating that it is a question of fact and its decision is not liable to be reviewed in an appeal by special leave.

The appellant was not entitled to a separate notice under the proviso to section 99 before a finding of a corrupt practice was recorded against him, because the finding related to the very payments which were the subject-matter of the enquiry in the election petition, where he already had an opportunity to be heard.
The appellant failed to show any ground for the Supreme Court to differ from the Tribunal's factual conclusion that the payments in question were election expenses and not innocent donations.
why_respondent_won: The Supreme Court's jurisdiction in an appeal by special leave does not extend to reviewing a Tribunal's findings of fact, such as the commencement of candidature.

The law, as previously interpreted by the Court, does not require a redundant second notice for a charge of corrupt practice when that exact charge was already fully litigated during the election petition hearing itself.
